newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: China set to veto Guatemala peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: China set to veto Guatemala peacekeepers.

text.p: China said on Friday it would veto a resolution authorizing 155 peacekeepers for Guatemala as the Security Council prepared for a vote in an apparent effort to embarrass Beijing publicly.
China had urged concessions from Guatemala on its diplomatic ties with Taiwan and said a letter from the Central American country on the issue was unsatisfactory.
Beijing's U.N. spokesman Chen Ranfeng told reporters that if council members insisted on a vote, "we will vote against." It would be China's first council veto in 24 years.

Despite China's vow to use its veto, the Security Council decided to call a meeting anyway on the resolution sponsored by the United States among others. It would allow the U.N. military observers to be in Guatemala for three months as part of a U.N.-brokered peace plan signed on Dec. 29. in Guatemala City.

Beijing has used its veto only twice in the Security Council since it unseated nationalist China and took its seat in 1971. One was on Aug. 25, 1972, to block the membership of Bangladesh in the United Nations and the second was shortly afterward, on Sept. 10, in connection with an amendment to a Middle East resolution.

Beijing considers Taiwan a rebel province and the two have been bitter political rivals since they were separated at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949. It has sought to push Taipei into diplomatic isolation in its quest to bring the island under communist control.
Guatemala has diplomatic relations with Taiwan, which gives it considerable economic aid.

"For the Chinese people, maintaining their national sovereignty and territorial integrity is the most important thing," Chen said, adding that Beijing also was particularly annoyed at the appearance of Taiwan's foreign minister, John Chang, at the Dec. 29 ceremonies in Guatemala City.

China also does not want Guatemala to join other states in requesting that United Nations membership for Taiwan be put on the General Assembly's agenda. Beijing succeeded in having Haiti refrain from this action last year after threatening several vetoes against the peacekeeping operation there.

Under military provisions of the peace accord, Guatemala's army will redeploy units to specified locations after which troops from the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) move to eight assembly points. The peace pact ended 36 years of a brutal civil war.
The unarmed U.N. military observers are to verify a cease-fire and patrol security zone assembly points.
Pedro Lamport, Guatemala's ambassador to Washington, told reporters China should take responsibility for its decision in front of the world community.
"We will find other mechanisms," he said. "There are other institutions in Latin America."
Diplomats said that the Organization for American States might take over the peacekeeping mission, an action that would not require Security Council approval.

"It would be a shame though that after so many years of U.N. accompaniment that the last phase, which is the beginning of the compliance of the agreement, the United Nations is deprived of that privilege," Lamport added.

"We have had extremely positive relationships with Tawian for more than 40 years," he added. "We are not a country which is going to change the friendship immediately. We are not going to change our friendship with Taiwan."
